newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico reserve hike costly, but economists unfazed.
newsitem.headline: Mexico reserve hike costly, but economists unfazed.

text.p: The sharp rise in Mexico's international reserves is proving costly to the government, but economists are so far not ringing alarm bells.

Last week, the government's Exchange Commission announced that it increased the amount of its dollar put option auction for August to $500 million, with the possibility of a second auction for the same amount during the month.
The government has said it was concerned about the appreciation of the robust peso, but the increase in the dollar puts will continue to add to the burgeoning reserves.
The accumulation of reserves has a price, though.
"It is a difficult decision. I would like to see the reserves a little higher even if that implies a cost," said Santander Investment economist Hector Chavez.
"Considering the level at which reserves were at and the reserves it (Banco de Mexico) has accumulated, I would think it could accumulate more," he said.
In its annual report released in January, the central bank forecast an increase in net international assets of at least $2.50 billion during 1997.
But it has surpassed that amount easily.

As of July 25, net international assets had risen $8.871 billion from the start of the year, increasing to a total of $15.184 billion. Reserves, assets plus mainly IMF funds, rose to $22.512 billion on the same date.
The put option scheme, revenues from state-owned Petroleos Mexicanos, and federal government borrowing from abroad have all added the cash mountain.
Banco de Mexico has a policy of sterilizing incoming funds to keep the monetary base, basically coins and bills in circulation, from exploding.
"Not a small sum of money, but with our assumption of a fiscal deficit in 1997 totalling 1.4 percent of GDP, not a major addition to fiscal red ink either, in our view," Brown wrote.

Bear Stearns economist David Malpass said in a report that Mexico could still accumulate more reserves, citing the fact that reserves started at a low level and they are being accumulated in addition to interest rate cuts.
"Fiscal issues are not high on a list of Mexico's economic problems, so paying the carrying costs of higher international reserves may be a good investment," Malpass added.

Central bank governor Miguel Mancera said earlier this year that, while good reserve levels give a sense of security to foreign investors, they do have a cost and should not be allowed to grow indefinitely.
He suggested that once the central bank had decided it had accumulated enough reserves, it could halt the dollar put auctions.
